translations.text: For we take this testimony into account, even though limiting his universal sovereignty to the kingship of Israel might seem to lessen the glory of his kingship.
That is not so. Rather, the inscription written on the cross in a twofold manner [?] declares his rule over all, since it does not add:
"He is king of Israel only." The wording simply testified to his rule over the Jews, and through this wording it joined to it a silent confession of his universal sovereignty.
For the king of the whole earth certainly also has kingship over a part of it.
Solomon's zeal for judging justly points to the true judge of the whole world, for he says:
"The Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son," and: "I can do nothing of myself, but as I hear, I judge, and my judgment is just."
For this is the highest standard of just judgment: that one judges those on trial not on one's own authority, nor out of any leniency or favour,
but first hears the case of those on trial, and only then gives sentence on them.
For this reason the power of God admits, about a certain matter: "I cannot do it," because truth cannot pervert judgment apart from justice.
That the Lord is from the seed of David according to the flesh has been confessed from the beginning through the promise made to David.
Let us now leave aside the many other figures and hurry our discussion along.
The mystery of this Indian queen will become clear to the intelligent: it proclaims the wonders of the Gospel.
It tells how she left the kingdom of India, crossed such great regions and distances, and came to Solomon out of love for his wisdom,
and honoured the king with precious stones, gold and fragrant spices. Understand this as follows:
Who would not know that the church of the Indian Gentiles was formerly black and Indian because of idolatry,
while it had not yet become a church, and was very far removed from the knowledge of the true God by the distance of ignorance?
But when "the grace of God appeared," wisdom shone forth, and the true light spread its rays on those sitting in darkness and in the shadows of death,
then the eyes of the Israelites were pained at seeing the light, and they became estranged from sharing in the good things.
But the Indians from among the Gentiles came to faith. Those who were once far off became near, and they washed away their Indianness with the water of the mystery.
So India was the first to stretch out her hand to God and offer the gifts of the King.
These gifts are the fragrant spices of devotion to God, the gold of knowledge of God, and the precious stones of fulfilling the commandments and the virtues.
From here on it is time to set about interpreting the divinely inspired words before us and to reveal their hidden meaning.
For it says: "King Solomon made himself a palanquin from the wood of Lebanon.
He made its pillars of silver and its curved vault of gold, its ascent of purple, its floor a stone pavement, love from the daughters of Jerusalem."
which drinks the rain that comes upon it. And another man is also created, renewed through the second birth in the image and likeness of the Creator.
And another nature becomes a luminary, concerning whom he says: "You are the lights of the world," and "that you may shine as lights in the world."
And no small multitude of stars shines in that firmament of faith. And this is not what is marvelous, that a multitude of stars shines in this new world,
which God counts and calls by name; rather, it is that the Creator of such stars writes their names in the heavens.
For thus the Creator of this new creation said to his own luminaries: "Your names are written in heaven."
And this alone is not what is marvelous, that a multitude of stars is created in it by the Word; but many suns also rise in it,
which light up the world with the brightness of good works. For thus that Creator said to such suns:
"Thus let your light shine before men," and: "Then the righteous will shine forth as luminaries."
And just as one who looks at this visible world and comes to know the true Wisdom through these manifest beauties
perceives through these things that have been described the invisible beauty and that abyss of wisdom whose depth created the beauty and the nature of these existing things,
so also one who looks at this new heaven and earth of the Church's creation sees in it
him who is all in all, and through the things our nature can grasp and attain he comes to understand those that are invisible and cannot be grasped.
And since at this point the virgin souls come before the soul that has reached perfection, so that she may tell them about the Beloved,

for this reason, through the things in which he was revealed to us as Savior, she portrays to the virgins the signs of the one they seek. She shows the whole Church to be the one body of the Bridegroom, and her own
understanding she depicts and signifies through the beauty of each member. By naming these one by one she completes the beauty of the whole body.
And she takes the starting point of her teaching from the structure of our bodies, just as Matthew also did, who began from Abraham and David to recount the mystery of the Incarnation
by genealogy; and to the great John was reserved, through the portrayal of such members, the account of the birth without beginning and the gospel of the Word who was from the beginning.
So too the bride, through such understandings, makes the virgins wise and teaches them that our mind cannot ascend to what is inaccessible and invisible
unless we first hold fast by faith to what was revealed; and the revelation is a matter of the nature of the flesh. For when she says:
"My kinsman is white and ruddy," she portrays the honor and the property of the flesh by mingling these two colors. And she used this same image above as well,
when she called him an apple, whose coloring, by its twofold mingling, signifies this same thing.
For the apple is white and red: the whiteness portrays the flesh, and the coloring portrays the blood.
